title: Score Spread When Cutting Into K Runs
statement:
You have a row of parcels with weights weights[0..n-1] and you must cut the row into exactly k non-empty contiguous runs, keeping the original order. Every parcel belongs to exactly one run.

A run from index i to index j costs weights[i] + weights[j] (a run of one parcel costs 2 · weights[i]). The score of a cutting is the sum of its runs' costs.

Return the difference between the largest and the smallest score over all possible cuttings.

examples.why: Cutting after the 1 scores (1 + 1) + (4 + 3) = 9, the minimum. Cutting after the 5 scores (1 + 5) + (3 + 3) = 12, the maximum. 12 − 9 = 3.
Cutting between the two 1s gives 6 + 6 = 12; cutting next to either 5 gives 16. The heaviest parcels are not what matters, the pair at the cut is.
With k = n there is only one way to cut, so the largest and smallest scores are the same.

hints: Write out the score of one cutting. The first and the last parcel always count. What does each cut add?

A cut between positions i and i + 1 ends one run at i and starts the next at i + 1, so it adds weights[i] + weights[i + 1]. The score is weights[0] + weights[n − 1] plus the sum over the k − 1 cuts you choose.
Compute the n − 1 adjacent pair sums and sort them. The largest score takes the k − 1 biggest pairs, the smallest takes the k − 1 smallest. The fixed ends cancel in the difference.

explain.intuition:
Look at what one cut contributes. Cutting between i and i + 1 makes weights[i] the last parcel of one run and weights[i + 1] the first parcel of the next, so it adds exactly weights[i] + weights[i + 1] to the score. Everything else is fixed: the very first and very last parcel always count once.

So a cutting is just a choice of k − 1 gaps out of n − 1, and the score is a constant plus the sum of the chosen gaps' pair sums. The choices do not interact, which makes this a plain selection problem: the maximum picks the k − 1 largest pair sums and the minimum the k − 1 smallest. The constant cancels when you subtract.
steps: Add up the last k − 1 entries and the first k − 1 entries.
Return the first sum minus the second.
pitfalls: Picking the heaviest single parcels instead of the heaviest adjacent pairs. The second example has its heavy parcels at the ends, where they always count anyway.
Choosing k pairs instead of k − 1. k runs need only k − 1 cuts.
Overflow in languages with 32-bit ints: the sums reach about 2 · 10¹⁴. JavaScript numbers and Python ints are safe here.

solutions.title: Try every set of cuts
solutions.idea: Enumerate every choice of k − 1 gaps, compute the score of the runs directly, and track the minimum and maximum.

solutions.title: Sort the adjacent pair sums
solutions.idea: Each cut adds the pair of parcels around it. Take the k − 1 largest pair sums for the maximum and the k − 1 smallest for the minimum.

followups: Return the actual cut positions for the maximum score, not just the spread.
Can you avoid the full sort when k is tiny compared with n?
